reminder: A plane wave is a [function](c:function) $c\,e^{ik\cdot x}$ whose phase is constant on every hyperplane perpendicular to $k$.
definition: A plane wave on [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a [function](c:function) $\psi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{C}$ with $\psi(x)=c\,e^{ik\cdot x}$. It uses the [exponential function](c:exponential-function), a [complex number](c:complex-number) $c$ as amplitude and a wave vector $k\in\mathbb{R}^n$. With a time variable the form is $\psi(x,t)=c\,e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}$ for a frequency $\omega\in\mathbb{R}$, and the phase $k\cdot x-\omega t$ is constant on each hyperplane perpendicular to $k$.
examples: $e^{ix}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is a plane wave with $k=1$, and its real part $\cos x$ is a real plane wave.
$e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}$ solves the wave equation $\partial_t^2\psi=c_0^2\,\Delta\psi$ when $\omega^2=c_0^2|k|^2$.
Non-example: the spherical wave $e^{ik|x|}/|x|$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$ has spheres, not planes, as wave fronts.

reminder: A Poincaré metric is a conformally compact [Einstein metric](c:einstein-metric) with $\mathrm{Ric}=-n\,g$ on the interior of a manifold with boundary.
definition: Let $M$ be a manifold of dimension $n$ with a conformal class $[g]$. A Poincaré metric for $(M,[g])$ is a [Riemannian](c:riemannian-manifold) metric $g_+$ on the interior of a [manifold with boundary](c:manifold-with-boundary) $\bar X$ of dimension $n+1$ with $\partial\bar X=M$, and $g_+$ is an [Einstein metric](c:einstein-metric) with [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) $\mathrm{Ric}(g_+)=-n\,g_+$. It is conformally compact: for a boundary defining function $\rho$, the metric $\rho^2g_+$ extends smoothly to $\bar X$ and restricts on $M$ to a representative of $[g]$.
examples: The [hyperbolic metric](c:hyperbolic-metric) $4|dx|^2/(1-|x|^2)^2$ on the open unit ball of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is a Poincaré metric, and its conformal infinity is the round sphere.
The half-space metric $(dx_0^2+|dx|^2)/x_0^2$ on $\{x_0>0\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is a Poincaré metric for the flat conformal class on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Non-example: the flat metric on the open ball does not satisfy $\mathrm{Ric}=-n\,g$, and it does not blow up at the boundary.

steps: Start with an [Einstein metric](c:einstein-metric) $g_+$ on the interior of a [manifold with boundary](c:manifold-with-boundary) of dimension $n+1$.
Fix the Einstein constant to be $-n$, so that $\mathrm{Ric}(g_+)=-n\,g_+$.
Add the condition that $\rho^2g_+$ extends smoothly to the boundary for a defining function $\rho$.
Then $g_+$ is a Poincaré metric, and $\rho^2g_+$ restricted to the boundary gives its conformal class.
links.why: It shows that a Poincaré metric is an Einstein metric plus a conformal boundary condition.

steps: Take the open unit ball with the [hyperbolic metric](c:hyperbolic-metric) $g_+=4|dx|^2/(1-|x|^2)^2$.
It has constant sectional curvature $-1$, so $\mathrm{Ric}(g_+)=-n\,g_+$.
With $\rho=(1-|x|^2)/2$ we get $\rho^2g_+=|dx|^2$, which extends to the closed ball.
So $g_+$ is a Poincaré metric, and its conformal infinity is the round sphere.
links.why: It shows that hyperbolic space is the model case that general Poincaré metrics copy near the boundary.

reminder: A pole of a function $f$ is an [isolated singularity](c:isolated-singularity) where $|f(z)|$ tends to infinity.
definition: Let $z_0$ be an [isolated singularity](c:isolated-singularity) of a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $f$. The point $z_0$ is a pole when $|f(z)|\to\infty$ as $z\to z_0$. Equivalently, $f(z)=g(z)/(z-z_0)^m$ near $z_0$ with $g$ holomorphic, $g(z_0)\neq0$ and an integer $m\ge1$, the order of the pole, and the [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) of $f$ at $z_0$ has finitely many negative powers.
examples: $1/z$ has a pole of order $1$ at $0$, and $1/(z-1)^2$ has a pole of order $2$ at $1$.
$1/\sin z$ has a simple pole at every point $k\pi$ with $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.
Non-example: $e^{1/z}$ has an isolated singularity at $0$ that is not a pole, because $e^{1/z}\to0$ as $z\to0$ along the negative real axis.

steps: Take a function $f$ that is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on a punctured disc around $z_0$.
Then $z_0$ is an [isolated singularity](c:isolated-singularity) of $f$.
Add the condition that $|f(z)|\to\infty$ as $z\to z_0$.
Then $z_0$ is a pole, and the Laurent series has only finitely many negative powers.
links.why: It shows that a pole is the isolated singularity where the function blows up, so its Laurent series has a finite principal part.

reminder: For a conic with bilinear form $B$, the polar of a point $P$ is the line of all points $X$ with $B(P,X)=0$.
definition: Let $C$ be a non-degenerate [conic section](c:conic-section) in the [projective plane](c:projective-plane) with equation $Q(X)=0$, where $Q(X)=B(X,X)$ for a symmetric [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $B$. The polar of a point $P$ is the [line](c:line) $\{X: B(P,X)=0\}$, and $P$ is the pole of that line. If $P$ lies on $C$, its polar is the [tangent line](c:tangent-line) to $C$ at $P$.
examples: For the unit circle $x^2+y^2=1$, the polar of $(a,b)$ is the line $ax+by=1$; for $(2,0)$ it is the line $x=1/2$.
A point of the conic has the tangent as its polar; for $(1,0)$ on the unit circle the polar is $x=1$.
Non-example: for the degenerate conic $xy=0$, the vertex $(0:0:1)$ has no polar line, because $B(P,X)=0$ holds for every $X$.

reminder: A polygon is a plane figure bounded by a closed chain of finitely many straight [line segments](c:line-segment).
definition: A polygon is the part of the [plane](c:plane) bounded by a simple [closed curve](c:closed-curve) that consists of $n\ge3$ [line segments](c:line-segment), its edges. Consecutive edges meet only at a shared [vertex](c:vertex), and edges that are not consecutive do not meet.
examples: A triangle, a square and a regular hexagon are polygons with $3$, $4$ and $6$ vertices.
An L-shaped figure with six edges is a polygon that is not convex.
Non-example: a bow-tie chain of four segments crosses itself, so it does not bound a simple polygon.

steps: Take a [triangle](c:triangle) with vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ that do not lie on one line.
Its sides $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$ are line segments that form a closed chain.
The sides meet only at the shared vertices, so the chain is simple.
So the triangle is a polygon with $n=3$.
links.why: It shows that a triangle is the polygon with the fewest vertices.

steps: Take a [regular polygon](c:regular-polygon) with $n$ vertices.
Its $n$ sides are line segments that form a simple closed chain.
So it is a polygon.
The regular case adds that all sides have equal length and all angles are equal.
links.why: It shows that regularity is an extra condition on a polygon, not a different kind of figure.

reminder: A polymorphic operation works at more than one [type](c:type), under one name or with one uniform definition.
definition: In a typed language, an operation shows polymorphism when one name or one definition serves more than one [type](c:type). Ad hoc polymorphism uses one name for different [functions](c:function), one for each type, as in overloading. Parametric polymorphism uses one definition that acts the same way at every type, for example at the [function type](c:function-type) $\forall\alpha.\ \alpha\to\alpha$.
examples: The identity function has the parametric type $\forall\alpha.\ \alpha\to\alpha$ and works at every type $\alpha$.
The symbol $+$ is ad hoc polymorphic: it adds integers by one rule and floating-point numbers by another rule.
Non-example: $\mathrm{succ}:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ works at one type only, so it is monomorphic.

reminder: A polynomial congruence $f(x)\equiv0\pmod m$ asks for the integers $x$ for which $m$ divides $f(x)$.
definition: Let $f$ be a [polynomial](c:polynomial) with [integer](c:integer) coefficients and let $m\ge2$ be an integer. The polynomial congruence $f(x)\equiv0\pmod m$ asks for the integers $x$ such that $m$ divides $f(x)$, see [divisibility](c:divisibility). Its solutions count as classes in [modular arithmetic](c:modular-arithmetic) modulo $m$, because $x+m$ is a solution exactly when $x$ is a solution.
examples: $x^2+1\equiv0\pmod5$ has the two solution classes $x\equiv2$ and $x\equiv3$.
$x^2\equiv1\pmod8$ has four solution classes $1,3,5,7$, more than the degree $2$, because $8$ is not prime.
Non-example: $2^x\equiv1\pmod7$ is not a polynomial congruence, because the unknown $x$ sits in an exponent.

reminder: A polynomial differential form on a simplex is a [differential form](c:differential-form) whose coefficients are polynomials in the barycentric coordinates.
definition: On the standard $n$-[simplex](c:simplex) $\Delta^n$ with barycentric coordinates $t_0,\dots,t_n$, a polynomial differential form of degree $p$ is a [differential form](c:differential-form) $\sum_I f_I\,dt_I$ whose coefficients $f_I$ are [polynomials](c:polynomial) in the $t_i$, with rational numbers as coefficients in Sullivan's setting. These forms are closed under $d$ and under restriction to faces, so they give a simplicial version of the [de Rham complex](c:de-rham-complex).
examples: On $\Delta^1$ with $t_0+t_1=1$, the $1$-form $t_0\,dt_1$ and the $0$-form $t_0t_1$ are polynomial forms.
The differential of a polynomial form is again polynomial: $d(t_0t_1)=t_1\,dt_0+t_0\,dt_1$.
Non-example: $e^{t_1}\,dt_1$ on $\Delta^1$ is a smooth form, but its coefficient is not a polynomial.

steps: Take a polynomial differential form $\omega=\sum_I f_I\,dt_I$ on $\Delta^n$.
Each coefficient $f_I$ is a polynomial, so it is a smooth function.
So $\omega$ is a smooth [differential form](c:differential-form) on the simplex.
The special case adds that every coefficient is a polynomial, which makes the whole complex algebraic.
links.why: It shows that polynomial forms are smooth forms with an algebraic restriction, so the de Rham operations still apply.

reminder: The Pontryagin ring of an [H-space](c:h-space) $X$ is its [homology](c:homology) with the product that the multiplication of $X$ induces.
definition: Let $X$ be an [H-space](c:h-space) with multiplication $\mu:X\times X\to X$ and let $k$ be a field. The Pontryagin ring is the [ordinary homology](c:ordinary-homology) $H_*(X;k)$ with the product $a\cdot b=\mu_*(a\times b)$, where $\times$ is the cross product into $H_*(X\times X;k)$. If $\mu$ is associative up to homotopy, as for a [topological group](c:topological-group) or a [loop space](c:loop-space), this product makes $H_*(X;k)$ an associative graded [ring](c:ring).
examples: For the circle group $S^1$, the Pontryagin ring $H_*(S^1;k)$ is the exterior algebra on one class of degree $1$.
For the loop space $\Omega S^{n+1}$ with $n\ge1$, the Pontryagin ring $H_*(\Omega S^{n+1};\mathbb{Z})$ is the tensor algebra on one generator of degree $n$.
Non-example: the sphere $S^2$ has no H-space multiplication, so it has no Pontryagin ring.

reminder: The Pontryagin dual of a [locally compact abelian group](c:locally-compact-abelian-group) $G$ is the group of continuous homomorphisms from $G$ to the circle.
definition: Let $G$ be a [locally compact abelian group](c:locally-compact-abelian-group). Its Pontryagin dual $\widehat G$ is the set of continuous [group homomorphisms](c:group-homomorphism) $\chi:G\to S^1$ into the [circle group](c:circle-group), with pointwise multiplication and the [compact-open topology](c:compact-open-topology). The elements of $\widehat G$ are the characters of $G$.
examples: The dual of $\mathbb{Z}$ is the circle: the integer $n$ pairs with $z\in S^1$ by $z^n$.
The dual of $\mathbb{R}$ is $\mathbb{R}$: the number $\xi$ gives the character $x\mapsto e^{i\xi x}$.
Non-example: homomorphisms $\mathbb{R}\to S^1$ that are not continuous exist, but they do not belong to the dual of $\mathbb{R}$.

reminder: The positive square root of a [positive operator](c:positive-operator) $A$ is the unique positive operator $B$ with $B^2=A$.
definition: Let $A$ be a [positive operator](c:positive-operator), for example a [positive semidefinite matrix](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix). Its positive square root $\sqrt A$ is the unique positive operator $B$ with $B^2=A$. If $A=\sum_i\lambda_iP_i$ is the spectral decomposition, then $\sqrt A=\sum_i\sqrt{\lambda_i}\,P_i$, where each $\sqrt{\lambda_i}\ge0$ is the usual [square root](c:square-root).
examples: $\sqrt{\mathrm{diag}(4,9)}=\mathrm{diag}(2,3)$.
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}5&4\\4&5\end{pmatrix}$ the positive square root is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, because its square is $A$ and its eigenvalues $3$ and $1$ are positive.
Non-example: $\mathrm{diag}(2,-3)$ squares to $\mathrm{diag}(4,9)$, but it has a negative eigenvalue, so it is not the positive square root.

steps: Take a number $a\ge0$ and view it as a $1\times1$ matrix.
This matrix is positive semidefinite.
Its positive square root is the $1\times1$ matrix $\sqrt a\ge0$.
So the matrix case contains the real [square root](c:square-root) of a nonnegative number.
links.why: It shows that the positive square root of an operator extends the familiar nonnegative root of a number.

reminder: The $k$-th power sum of $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is the [symmetric polynomial](c:symmetric-polynomial) $p_k=x_1^k+\dots+x_n^k$.
definition: For an integer $k\ge1$ and variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$, the $k$-th power sum is the [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p_k=x_1^k+x_2^k+\dots+x_n^k$. It is a [symmetric polynomial](c:symmetric-polynomial) of degree $k$. If the $x_i$ are the roots of a polynomial, $p_k$ is the sum of the $k$-th powers of its [roots](c:root-of-a-polynomial).
examples: For the roots $1$ and $2$ of $x^2-3x+2$ we get $p_1=3$ and $p_2=5$.
Non-example: $xy+xz+yz$ is symmetric, but it is the elementary symmetric polynomial $e_2$, not a power sum.

steps: Take the power sum $p_k=x_1^k+\dots+x_n^k$.
Swap two variables $x_i$ and $x_j$.
The terms $x_i^k$ and $x_j^k$ trade places, and all other terms stay.
So the sum does not change, and $p_k$ is a [symmetric polynomial](c:symmetric-polynomial).
links.why: It shows that power sums live in the ring of symmetric polynomials, where Newton's identities relate them to the elementary ones.

reminder: The presheaf topos of a [small category](c:small-category) $C$ is the category of functors $C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Set}$ with natural transformations.
definition: For a [small category](c:small-category) $C$, the presheaf topos $\widehat C$ is the [functor category](c:functor-category) $[C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Set}]$. Its objects are [presheaves](c:presheaf) on $C$, its morphisms are [natural transformations](c:natural-transformation), and it is a [topos](c:topos).
examples: For $C$ the category with one object and only its identity, $\widehat C$ is the category $\mathrm{Set}$.
For $C=\Delta$, the simplex category, $\widehat C$ is the category of simplicial sets.
Non-example: the category of finite sets is a topos but not a presheaf topos, because it has no infinite coproducts.

steps: Take a [small category](c:small-category) $C$ and give it the trivial topology, in which only maximal sieves cover.
Then every presheaf on $C$ satisfies the sheaf condition.
So the category of [sheaves](c:sheaf) on $C$ is all of $[C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Set}]$.
Hence every presheaf topos is a [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos).
links.why: It shows that presheaf toposes are the Grothendieck toposes with no gluing condition.

reminder: The prime counting function $\pi(x)$ gives the number of [prime numbers](c:prime-number) that are at most $x$.
definition: The prime counting function is the [function](c:function) $\pi$ that sends a [real number](c:real-number) $x$ to the [natural number](c:natural-number) $\pi(x)=\#\{p\le x: p\text{ is prime}\}$, the count of [prime numbers](c:prime-number) not larger than $x$. It is a step function that jumps by $1$ at each prime.
examples: $\pi(10)=4$, because the primes up to $10$ are $2,3,5,7$.
$\pi(1)=0$ and $\pi(2.5)=1$, so $\pi$ takes real arguments.
Non-example: $x/\ln x$ is close to $\pi(x)$ for large $x$, but it is not equal to $\pi(x)$; for instance $10/\ln10\approx4.34$.

reminder: A prime factor of a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number) that divides $n$.
definition: Let $n$ be a [natural number](c:natural-number). A prime factor of $n$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$ that [divides](c:divisibility) $n$, that is, $kp=n$ for some natural number $k$.
examples: The prime factors of $12$ are $2$ and $3$.
A prime number $p$ has exactly one prime factor, which is $p$ itself.
Non-example: $4$ divides $12$, but $4$ is not prime, so it is not a prime factor of $12$.

steps: Take a natural number $n$ and a number $p$ such that $p$ [divides](c:divisibility) $n$.
Divisibility only says that $kp=n$ for some natural number $k$.
Add the condition that $p$ is a prime number.
Then $p$ is a prime factor of $n$.
links.why: It shows that a prime factor is a divisor that cannot be split further.

reminder: In a [Dedekind domain](c:dedekind-domain), every nonzero proper [ideal](c:ideal) is a product of [prime ideals](c:prime-ideal) in exactly one way.
definition: Let $R$ be a [Dedekind domain](c:dedekind-domain) and $I$ a nonzero proper [ideal](c:ideal) of $R$. The prime ideal factorization of $I$ is the equation $I=P_1^{e_1}\cdots P_r^{e_r}$ with distinct nonzero [prime ideals](c:prime-ideal) $P_i$ and exponents $e_i\ge1$. The $P_i$ and the $e_i$ are unique up to the order of the factors.
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}$, the ideal $(12)$ factors as $(2)^2(3)$.
In $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, the ideal $(5)$ factors as $(2+i)(2-i)$.
Non-example: $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ factors an element, not an ideal into prime ideals, and $2$, $3$ and $1\pm\sqrt{-5}$ do not generate prime ideals.

steps: Take the [prime factorization](c:prime-factorization) of an integer $n\ge2$, written $n=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_r^{e_r}$.
The ring $\mathbb{Z}$ is a Dedekind domain, and its nonzero prime ideals are the ideals $(p)$ with $p$ prime.
The factorization of $n$ gives $(n)=(p_1)^{e_1}\cdots(p_r)^{e_r}$.
So prime factorization of integers is the case $R=\mathbb{Z}$.
links.why: It shows that unique factorization of ideals is the version of unique prime factorization that survives in rings of integers.

reminder: The prime spectrum of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ is the set of its [prime ideals](c:prime-ideal) with the Zariski topology.
definition: For a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, the prime spectrum $\mathrm{Spec}\,R$ is the set of all [prime ideals](c:prime-ideal) of $R$. Its closed sets are the sets $V(I)=\{\mathfrak p:\mathfrak p\supseteq I\}$ for ideals $I$ of $R$, which is the [Zariski topology](c:zariski-topology) and makes $\mathrm{Spec}\,R$ a [topological space](c:topological-space).
examples: $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}$ has one point $(p)$ for each prime $p$ and one more point $(0)$, which is dense.
For a field $k$, $\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ is a single point $(0)$.
Non-example: the set of maximal ideals of $\mathbb{Z}$ leaves out the prime ideal $(0)$, so it is not $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: Take an [affine variety](c:affine-variety) $V$ over an algebraically closed field $k$, with coordinate ring $k[V]$.
By the Nullstellensatz, the points of $V$ correspond to the maximal ideals of $k[V]$.
Add all other [prime ideals](c:prime-ideal) of $k[V]$ to get $\mathrm{Spec}\,k[V]$ with the Zariski topology.
Then $V$ is the subspace of closed points of $\mathrm{Spec}\,k[V]$.
links.why: It shows how the prime spectrum extends a variety by points for its subvarieties.

reminder: The $k$-th principal minor of a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) is the [determinant](c:determinant) of its upper left $k\times k$ block.
definition: Let $A=(a_{ij})$ be an $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$. For $k=1,\dots,n$, the $k$-th principal minor is $\Delta_k=\det(a_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le k}$, the [determinant](c:determinant) of the upper left $k\times k$ block. Some texts also call the determinant of any submatrix with the same row and column indices a principal minor; the upper left block gives the leading ones.
examples: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&3&1\\0&1&4\end{pmatrix}$ the principal minors are $\Delta_1=2$, $\Delta_2=5$ and $\Delta_3=18$.
The last principal minor $\Delta_n$ is always $\det A$.
Non-example: for the same $A$, the minor on rows $1,2$ and columns $2,3$ equals $1$, but it is not principal, because its rows and columns differ.

reminder: A principal submatrix of a matrix $A$ keeps the entries $A_{ij}$ with both $i$ and $j$ in the same index subset.
definition: Let $A=(A_{ij})_{i,j\in I}$ be a [matrix](c:matrix) indexed by a [set](c:set) $I$. For a [subset](c:subset) $I'\subseteq I$, the principal submatrix of $A$ on $I'$ is $(A_{ij})_{i,j\in I'}$. It uses the same index set for rows and columns, so it is a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) that keeps the diagonal entries $A_{ii}$ with $i\in I'$.
examples: Delete row $2$ and column $2$ of a $3\times3$ matrix: the $2\times2$ matrix on $I'=\{1,3\}$ is a principal submatrix.
The upper left $k\times k$ block is the principal submatrix on $I'=\{1,\dots,k\}$.
Non-example: deleting row $1$ and column $2$ leaves rows $\{2,3\}$ and columns $\{1,3\}$, which differ, so the result is not principal.

reminder: Probabilistic amplification runs a randomized algorithm many times with independent random bits and takes the majority answer, so the error becomes small.
definition: Let $A$ be a randomized [algorithm](c:algorithm) for a language in [BPP](c:bpp) that is correct with [probability](c:probability) at least $2/3$ on every input. Amplification runs $A$ for $t$ times with [independent](c:independent-random-variables) random bits and outputs the majority answer. By a Hoeffding bound the error is at most $e^{-t/18}$, so $t=O(n)$ runs give an error below $2^{-n}$.
examples: Run a $1/3$-error algorithm $t=100$ times and take the majority: the error is at most $e^{-100/18}<0.004$.
For one-sided error, accept when any run accepts: if one run succeeds with probability at least $1/2$, then $t$ runs fail with probability at most $2^{-t}$.
Non-example: running the algorithm $t$ times with the same random bits repeats one answer, so the error does not fall.

reminder: A probabilistically checkable proof lets a verifier read a few random positions of a [proof](c:proof) and still reject a false claim with high probability.
definition: A probabilistically checkable proof system for a language $L$ is a polynomial-time randomized [algorithm](c:algorithm) $V$, the verifier, that gets an input $x$ and random access to a [proof](c:proof) string $\pi$. It uses $r(n)$ random bits and reads $q(n)$ positions of $\pi$, and the languages with such systems form the [complexity class](c:complexity-class) $\mathrm{PCP}[r,q]$. If $x\in L$, some $\pi$ makes $V$ accept with [probability](c:probability) $1$; if $x\notin L$, every $\pi$ makes $V$ accept with probability at most $1/2$.
examples: Every language in [NP](c:np-complexity-class) has a trivial system with $r=0$: the verifier reads the whole certificate and checks it.
The PCP theorem says that every language in NP has a system with $r=O(\log n)$ random bits and $q=O(1)$ queries.
Non-example: a verifier that accepts some proof of a false statement with probability $0.9$ breaks the second condition, so it is not a probabilistically checkable proof system.

steps: Take a language $L$ in [NP](c:np-complexity-class) with a polynomial-time verifier $V$ and certificates $\pi$.
View $V$ as a verifier that uses $0$ random bits and reads the whole certificate.
Then $V$ accepts a good certificate with probability $1$ and rejects every certificate for $x\notin L$.
So $L$ has a probabilistically checkable proof system with $r=0$ and polynomially many queries.
links.why: It shows that the NP verifier is the case of no randomness, and the PCP theorem trades the full reading for a few random queries.

reminder: The product of two functions $f$ and $g$ is the function $fg$ with $(fg)(x)=f(x)\,g(x)$.
definition: Let $f$ and $g$ be [functions](c:function) from a set $X$ to the [real numbers](c:real-number), or to any commutative ring. Their product is the function $fg:X\to\mathbb{R}$ with $(fg)(x)=f(x)\,g(x)$ for every $x\in X$. The product is pointwise: it multiplies the values at each point.
examples: For $f(x)=x$ and $g(x)=\sin x$, the product is $(fg)(x)=x\sin x$.
The Leibniz formula $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$ gives the [derivative](c:derivative) of a product of differentiable functions.
Non-example: $\sin(x^2)$ is the composition of $\sin$ and $x^2$, not their product $x^2\sin x$.

reminder: A program is a finite description, in a formal language, of how to compute an output of a given [type](c:type).
definition: A program is a finite expression of a formal programming language that specifies a computation step by step. In the type-theoretic view, a program is a [term](c:term) of some [type](c:type), and its value is the output; a program of function type $A\to B$ computes a [function](c:function) from $A$ to $B$.
examples: $\lambda n.\,n+1$ is a program of type $\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ that adds one.
A sorting routine is a program of type $\mathrm{List}\,\mathbb{N}\to\mathrm{List}\,\mathbb{N}$.
Non-example: the sentence “return a sorted list” is a specification, not a program, because it gives no rule for the computation.

reminder: A projection is a canonical map from a [product](c:product) onto one of its factors.
definition: A [product](c:product) $X_1\times X_2$ in a [category](c:category) comes with maps $p_i:X_1\times X_2\to X_i$ and this [universal property](c:universal-property): every pair of maps $f_i:Z\to X_i$ equals $p_i\circ h$ for exactly one map $h:Z\to X_1\times X_2$. The maps $p_i$ are the projections. For sets with the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product), $p_i(x_1,x_2)=x_i$.
examples: For sets, $p_1:A\times B\to A$ sends $(a,b)$ to $a$.
For groups, the projection $G\times H\to G$ is a group homomorphism.
Non-example: the inclusion $A\to A\times B$, $a\mapsto(a,b_0)$, goes into the product, so it is not a projection.

reminder: A projection matrix is a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $P$ with $P^2=P$, and it is orthogonal when also $P^{\mathsf T}=P$.
definition: A projection matrix is a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $P$ that is [idempotent](c:idempotent), so $P^2=P$. It maps every vector onto the [image](c:image) of $P$, its column space, and it fixes the vectors of that space. It is an orthogonal projection when $P$ is also a [symmetric matrix](c:symmetric-matrix), and then $P=X(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}$ for any $X$ whose columns are a basis of the image.
examples: $\mathrm{diag}(1,0)$ projects $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto the $x$-axis.
$\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ projects orthogonally onto the line $y=x$.
$\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is a projection matrix that is not symmetric, so its projection is oblique.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ has square $\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$, which is not the matrix itself, so it is not idempotent.

steps: Take a [projection operator](c:projection-operator) $T$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, that is, a linear map with $T\circ T=T$.
Write $T$ as a matrix $P$ in the standard basis.
Composition of maps becomes matrix multiplication, so $P^2=P$.
So $P$ is a projection matrix, and each projection matrix gives such a map $v\mapsto Pv$.
links.why: It shows that a projection matrix is a projection operator written in coordinates.

reminder: A projection operator is a [linear map](c:linear-map) $P$ with $P\circ P=P$; on a Hilbert space it is also self-adjoint.
definition: A projection operator on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is a [linear map](c:linear-map) $P:V\to V$ with $P\circ P=P$, and it splits $V$ into the image and the kernel of $P$. On a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) one also asks that $P$ is a [self-adjoint operator](c:self-adjoint-operator). Then $P$ is the orthogonal projection onto the [closed subspace](c:closed-subspace) $\operatorname{im}P$.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^2$, $P(x,y)=(x,0)$ is a projection operator onto the $x$-axis.
On a Hilbert space, $Pv=\langle u,v\rangle u$ for a unit vector $u$ is the projection onto the line spanned by $u$; quantum theory writes it as $|u\rangle\langle u|$.
Non-example: the swap $T(x,y)=(y,x)$ has $T\circ T=\mathrm{id}\neq T$, so $T$ is not a projection operator.

steps: Take the [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection) $P$ of a Hilbert space $H$ onto a closed subspace $U$.
The map $P$ is linear and its image is $U$.
Each $u\in U$ satisfies $Pu=u$, so $P(Pv)=Pv$ for all $v$.
So $P$ is a projection operator, and the extra condition $P=P^*$ singles out the orthogonal ones.
links.why: It shows that an orthogonal projection is a projection operator with the extra self-adjointness condition.

steps: Take a [projection matrix](c:projection-matrix) $P$, so $P^2=P$.
The map $v\mapsto Pv$ is linear.
Applied twice, it gives $v\mapsto P^2v=Pv$, the same map.
So it is a projection operator on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
links.why: It shows that every projection matrix is a projection operator in coordinates.

reminder: An [object](c:object) $P$ is projective when every map from $P$ to the target of an [epimorphism](c:epi) lifts through that epimorphism.
definition: An [object](c:object) $P$ of a [category](c:category) is projective when, for every [epimorphism](c:epi) $e:A\to B$ and every morphism $f:P\to B$, there is a [lift](c:lift) $g:P\to A$ with $e\circ g=f$. Equivalently, the [hom-functor](c:hom-functor) $\mathrm{Hom}(P,-)$ sends epimorphisms to surjections.
examples: In the category of sets, every set is projective, by the axiom of choice.
In the category of modules over a ring, every free module is projective.

Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}/2$ is not projective among abelian groups, because the identity of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ does not lift through the surjection $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/2$, since $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z})=0$.

steps: Work in the category of modules over a ring $R$.
A morphism out of $P$ is a module map, and an epimorphism is a surjective module map.
The lifting condition says that every map $P\to B$ lifts through every surjection $A\to B$.
This is the usual definition of a [projective module](c:projective-module).
links.why: It shows that a projective module is a projective object in a category of modules.

reminder: The projective bundle $P(E)$ of a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) $E$ replaces each fibre $E_x$ by its [projective space](c:projective-space) $P(E_x)$.
definition: Let $E\to X$ be a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) with [zero section](c:zero-section). The projective bundle $P(E)$ is the quotient of $E$ minus its zero section by the [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation) $v\sim\lambda v$ for nonzero scalars $\lambda$, with the quotient topology. Its fibre over $x$ is the [projective space](c:projective-space) $P(E_x)$ of lines in $E_x$, and $P(E)\to X$ is a [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle).
examples: For the trivial bundle $X\times k^{n+1}$, the projective bundle is $X\times P^n$.
For the tangent bundle $TM$ of an $n$-manifold $M$, $P(TM)$ is the bundle of tangent directions, with fibre $P^{n-1}$.
Non-example: the sphere bundle of unit vectors in a real vector bundle is not $P(E)$, because it does not identify $v$ with $-v$; its fibre is $S^n$, not $\mathbb{RP}^n$.

steps: Take $X$ to be a point and $E=V$ a vector space.
The zero section is the origin, so $E$ minus its zero section is $V\setminus\{0\}$.
The relation $v\sim\lambda v$ gives the quotient that defines the [projective space](c:projective-space) $P(V)$.
So $P(V)$ is the projective bundle of $V$ over a point.
links.why: It shows that a projective bundle is a family of projective spaces over a base.

steps: Choose a local trivialization $E|_U\cong U\times k^{n+1}$ over an open set $U$.
It induces a bijection $P(E|_U)\cong U\times P^n$ that is compatible with the projection to $U$.
The transition functions act on $P^n$ through invertible linear maps.
So $P(E)\to X$ is a [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle) with fibre $P^n$.
links.why: It shows that a projective bundle has local product charts like any fibre bundle, with fibre a projective space.

reminder: A diagram $X:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}$ is projectively cofibrant when it has the left lifting property against all objectwise trivial fibrations.
definition: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a [cofibrantly generated model category](c:cofibrantly-generated-model-category) and $\mathcal{D}$ a small category. The [functor category](c:functor-category) $[\mathcal{D},\mathcal{C}]$ has the projective model structure, whose weak equivalences and fibrations are the natural transformations that are objectwise ones in $\mathcal{C}$. A [diagram](c:diagram) $X:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}$ is projectively cofibrant when it is a [cofibrant object](c:cofibrant-object) of this structure, that is, it lifts against every objectwise trivial fibration.
examples: For a discrete $\mathcal{D}$, a diagram is projectively cofibrant exactly when every value $X_d$ is cofibrant.
For the span $B\leftarrow A\to C$, the diagram is projectively cofibrant when $A$ is cofibrant and both maps out of $A$ are cofibrations.
Non-example: a span $B\leftarrow A\to C$ in which $A\to B$ is not a cofibration is not projectively cofibrant, even if $A$, $B$ and $C$ are all cofibrant.

steps: Take $\mathcal{D}$ to be the category with one object and only its identity morphism.
A diagram $X:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}$ is then just an object of $\mathcal{C}$.
The projective model structure on $[\mathcal{D},\mathcal{C}]$ is the given structure on $\mathcal{C}$.
So the projectively cofibrant diagrams are exactly the [cofibrant objects](c:cofibrant-object) of $\mathcal{C}$.
links.why: It shows that projectively cofibrant diagrams extend the idea of a cofibrant object from single objects to diagrams.

reminder: The proximal operator of a [convex function](c:convex-function) $f$ sends $x$ to the point $y$ that minimises $f(y)+\frac12\|x-y\|^2$.
definition: Let $f:H\to(-\infty,\infty]$ be a proper [convex function](c:convex-function) that is [lower semicontinuous](c:lower-semicontinuous-function) on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$, and let $\lambda>0$. The proximal operator is $\mathrm{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)=\arg\min_{y\in H}\bigl(f(y)+\tfrac1{2\lambda}\|x-y\|^2\bigr)$, where $\|\cdot\|$ is the [norm](c:norm) of $H$. The minimiser exists and is unique, and the minimum value is the [Moreau envelope](c:moreau-envelope) of $f$.
examples: For $f=0$, the proximal operator is the identity.
For $f(x)=|x|$ on $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathrm{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)=\mathrm{sign}(x)\max(|x|-\lambda,0)$, the soft threshold.
Non-example: for the nonconvex $f(y)=-|y|$ with $\lambda=1$ and $x=0$, both $y=1$ and $y=-1$ are minimisers, so there is no single value.

steps: Take a closed subspace $U$ of a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ and its indicator function $\iota_U$, which is $0$ on $U$ and $\infty$ outside.
The function $\iota_U$ is convex and lower semicontinuous.
Then $\mathrm{prox}_{\iota_U}(x)$ minimises $\|x-y\|$ over $y\in U$.
That minimiser is the [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection) of $x$ onto $U$.
links.why: It shows that the proximal operator extends the nearest-point projection from subspaces to arbitrary convex functions.

reminder: A pseudonatural transformation is a [lax natural transformation](c:lax-natural-transformation) whose comparison [2-morphisms](c:2-morphism) are all invertible.
definition: Let $F,G:\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}$ be [2-functors](c:2-functor) between [2-categories](c:2-category). A pseudonatural transformation $\alpha:F\Rightarrow G$ gives a 1-morphism $\alpha_b:Fb\to Gb$ for each object $b$, and an invertible [2-morphism](c:2-morphism) $\alpha_f$ between $Gf\circ\alpha_b$ and $\alpha_{b'}\circ Ff$ for each 1-morphism $f:b\to b'$. These cells are natural in $f$ and compatible with identities and composition, as for a [lax natural transformation](c:lax-natural-transformation).
examples: A natural transformation of ordinary functors is a pseudonatural transformation of the 2-functors between locally discrete 2-categories, with identity comparison cells.
A 2-natural transformation, where each $\alpha_f$ is an identity, is pseudonatural.
Non-example: a lax natural transformation with a non-invertible comparison cell $\alpha_f$ for some $f$ is lax but not pseudonatural.

steps: Start with a [lax natural transformation](c:lax-natural-transformation) $\alpha:F\Rightarrow G$.
It has components $\alpha_b$ and a comparison [2-morphism](c:2-morphism) $\alpha_f$ for each 1-morphism $f$.
Add the condition that every $\alpha_f$ is invertible.
Then $\alpha$ is a pseudonatural transformation.
links.why: It shows that pseudonaturality is laxness plus invertible comparison cells.

steps: Take a [natural transformation](c:natural-transformation) of functors between 1-categories, viewed as 2-categories with identity 2-morphisms only.
Its naturality squares commute, so take the identity 2-morphisms as comparison cells.
Identity cells are invertible and satisfy the compatibility conditions.
So the natural transformation is a pseudonatural transformation.
links.why: It shows that pseudonatural transformations extend natural transformations to 2-categories by weakening commuting squares.

reminder: A pure state is a [state](c:state-on-a-star-algebra) that is an [extreme point](c:extreme-point) of the convex set of all states.
definition: Let $A$ be a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra). Its [states](c:state-on-a-star-algebra) form a [convex set](c:convex-set). A state $\omega$ is pure when it is an extreme point of this set: if $\omega=t\omega_1+(1-t)\omega_2$ with states $\omega_i$ and $0<t<1$, then $\omega_1=\omega_2=\omega$.
examples: On the matrix algebra $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, the pure states are the vector states $\omega(a)=\langle\psi,a\psi\rangle$ with $\|\psi\|=1$.
On the commutative algebra $C(X)$ of continuous functions on a compact Hausdorff space, the pure states are the point evaluations $f\mapsto f(x)$.
Non-example: on $M_2(\mathbb{C})$, the state $\omega(a)=\tfrac12\mathrm{tr}(a)$ is the average of two vector states, so it is mixed and not pure.

steps: Start with a [state](c:state-on-a-star-algebra) $\omega$ on a C*-algebra $A$.
The set of all states is convex, so we can ask whether $\omega$ is a mixture of other states.
Add the condition that $\omega=t\omega_1+(1-t)\omega_2$ with $0<t<1$ forces $\omega_1=\omega_2=\omega$.
Then $\omega$ is a pure state.
links.why: It shows that a pure state is a state that is not a nontrivial mixture of other states.

steps: Take the convex set $S(A)$ of states of the algebra $A$.
An [extreme point](c:extreme-point) of $S(A)$ is a point that is not inside any open segment between two other points of $S(A)$.
The extreme points of $S(A)$ are by definition the pure states.
links.why: It shows that purity is extremality in the convex set of states.

reminder: A pushout of $B\leftarrow A\to C$ is the universal object that receives maps from $B$ and $C$ that agree on $A$.
definition: Let $f:A\to B$ and $g:A\to C$ be morphisms, that is, a [span](c:span). A pushout is the [colimit](c:colimit) of this span: an object $P$ with maps $i:B\to P$ and $j:C\to P$ such that $i\circ f=j\circ g$, see [commutative diagram](c:commutative-diagram). It has this [universal property](c:universal-property): every pair $u:B\to X$, $v:C\to X$ with $u\circ f=v\circ g$ equals $h\circ i$ and $h\circ j$ for exactly one $h:P\to X$.
examples: In sets, $P=(B\sqcup C)/{\sim}$ where $f(a)\sim g(a)$ for every $a\in A$.
Gluing two spaces along a common subspace $A$ is the pushout of the two inclusions of $A$; the wedge sum $X\vee Y$ is the pushout of $X\leftarrow\{*\}\to Y$.
Non-example: for non-empty $A$, the disjoint union $B\sqcup C$ is not a pushout, because it does not identify $f(a)$ with $g(a)$.

steps: Take the category $J$ with three objects $a$, $b$, $c$ and arrows $a\to b$ and $a\to c$.
A diagram of shape $J$ is a [span](c:span) $B\leftarrow A\to C$.
A [cocone](c:cocone) over it is a pair of maps out of $B$ and $C$ that agree on $A$.
The universal cocone is the pushout, so the pushout is the [colimit](c:colimit) of this diagram.
links.why: It shows that a pushout is a colimit over the smallest shape with a shared source.

steps: Take a pushout of $B\leftarrow A\to C$ in which $A$ is an initial object.
The maps $f$ and $g$ out of $A$ are then unique, so $i\circ f=j\circ g$ holds automatically.
The pushout is then universal among all pairs of maps out of $B$ and $C$, which is the [coproduct](c:coproduct).
links.why: It shows that the coproduct is a pushout over an initial object.

reminder: A Pythagorean triple is a triple of integers $(a,b,c)$ with $a^2+b^2=c^2$.
definition: A Pythagorean triple is a triple $(a,b,c)$ of integers, usually taken positive, that is a solution of the [Diophantine equation](c:diophantine-equation) $a^2+b^2=c^2$. It is primitive when $a$, $b$ and $c$ have no common factor greater than $1$. Such a triple gives the sides of a right triangle with [integer](c:integer) side lengths.
examples: $(3,4,5)$ and $(5,12,13)$ are primitive Pythagorean triples.
$(6,8,10)$ is a Pythagorean triple that is not primitive, because it is $2\cdot(3,4,5)$.
Non-example: $(2,3,4)$ fails, because $2^2+3^2=13$ and $4^2=16$.

reminder: A quadratic algebra is a graded algebra $T(V)/(R)$ with generators in degree $1$ and relations $R$ only in degree $2$.
definition: A (graded) quadratic algebra over a field $k$ is an $\mathbb{N}$-[graded algebra](c:graded-algebra) $A=T(V)/(R)$, where $T(V)$ is the [tensor algebra](c:tensor-algebra) of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ placed in degree $1$ and $R\subseteq V\otimes V$ is a set of quadratic relations. The [ideal](c:ideal) $(R)$ is generated by $R$, so $A_0=k$, $A_1=V$, and all relations sit in degree $2$.
examples: The polynomial algebra $k[x,y]=T(V)/(x\otimes y-y\otimes x)$ with $V=k\{x,y\}$ is quadratic.
The exterior algebra $\Lambda(V)=T(V)/(v\otimes v)$ is quadratic.
Non-example: $k[x]/(x^3)$ has the relation $x^3$ in degree $3$, so quadratic relations alone do not present it.

steps: Start with a [graded algebra](c:graded-algebra) $A$ that is generated by its degree $1$ part $A_1=V$ and has $A_0=k$.
Then $A$ is a quotient $T(V)/J$ of the tensor algebra by a homogeneous ideal $J$.
Add the condition that $J$ is generated by elements of degree $2$.
Then $A$ is a quadratic algebra.
links.why: It shows that a quadratic algebra is a graded algebra whose relations all have degree two.

steps: Take a [Koszul algebra](c:koszul-algebra) $A$ over a field $k$.
By definition it has generators in degree $1$ and relations in degree $2$.
So $A=T(V)/(R)$ is a quadratic algebra.
Koszulness adds the condition that the trivial module $k$ has a linear free resolution.
links.why: It shows that Koszul algebras are the quadratic algebras with a linear resolution of $k$.

reminder: A quadratic function is a [function](c:function) $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ with $a$, $b$, $c$ in a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring), usually with $a\neq0$.
definition: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring). A quadratic function on $R$ is a [function](c:function) $f:R\to R$ for which there are $a,b,c\in R$ with $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ for all $x\in R$. One usually asks that $a\neq0$, so that $f$ comes from a [polynomial](c:polynomial) of degree $2$.
examples: $f(x)=x^2-5x+6$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has the roots $2$ and $3$.
$f(x)=x^2$ is quadratic with $a=1$ and $b=c=0$.
Non-example: on $\mathbb{R}$, $x^3-x$ has three zeros, but a quadratic function with $a\neq0$ has at most two.

steps: Take $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ on a commutative ring $R$.
The expression $ax^2+bx+c$ is a [polynomial](c:polynomial) in $x$ with coefficients in $R$.
Add the condition that $a\neq0$, so the degree is exactly $2$.
Then $f$ is the function of a polynomial of degree $2$, a quadratic function.
links.why: It shows that a quadratic function is the function of a polynomial of degree two.

steps: Take $R$ to be the field of [real numbers](c:real-number).
Then $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ has real coefficients $a$, $b$, $c$ with $a\neq0$.
This $f$ is a [real quadratic function](c:real-quadratic-function).
links.why: It shows that the school case of real parabolas is one choice of the ring $R$.

reminder: A quantum channel is a [linear map](c:linear-map) on operators that is completely positive and preserves the trace.
definition: A quantum channel is a [linear map](c:linear-map) $\Phi$ between operators on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces that is a [completely positive map](c:completely-positive-map) and preserves the [trace](c:trace-of-a-matrix), so $\mathrm{tr}\,\Phi(\rho)=\mathrm{tr}\,\rho$. Complete positivity means that $\mathrm{id}_n\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every $n$. Hence a channel sends each [density operator](c:density-operator) to a density operator, even when it acts on one part of a larger system.
examples: Conjugation $\rho\mapsto U\rho U^*$ by a unitary matrix $U$ is a channel.
The partial trace $\mathrm{tr}_B$ from operators on $H_A\otimes H_B$ to operators on $H_A$ is a channel.
The bit-flip channel $\rho\mapsto(1-p)\rho+p\,X\rho X$ with the Pauli matrix $X$ is a channel.
Non-example: the transpose map $\rho\mapsto\rho^{\mathsf T}$ preserves the trace and is positive, but it is not completely positive.

steps: Start with a [completely positive map](c:completely-positive-map) $\Phi$ between operators on Hilbert spaces.
Add the condition $\mathrm{tr}\,\Phi(\rho)=\mathrm{tr}\,\rho$ for every operator $\rho$.
Then $\Phi$ sends density operators to density operators, also on every larger system.
So $\Phi$ is a quantum channel.
links.why: It shows that a channel is a completely positive map that conserves total probability.

steps: Take a unitary matrix $U$ and set $\Phi(\rho)=U\rho U^*$.
The map $\Phi$ is linear, and $\mathrm{tr}(U\rho U^*)=\mathrm{tr}\,\rho$.
The map $\Phi$ has the single Kraus operator $U$, so it is completely positive.
So each [unitary quantum channel](c:unitary-quantum-channel) is a quantum channel.
links.why: It shows that reversible quantum evolution is the special channel with one Kraus operator.

reminder: A quantum gate is a [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) on the state space of one or more qubits.
definition: A quantum gate on $n$ qubits is a [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) $U$ on the [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $(\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n}$. It maps each [quantum state](c:quantum-state) $\psi$, a unit vector, to the state $U\psi$, and it is reversible with inverse $U^*$.
examples: The Hadamard gate $H=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ acts on one qubit.
The CNOT gate acts on two qubits: it flips the second qubit when the first qubit is $1$.
Non-example: the projector $|0\rangle\langle0|$ is not a gate, because it is not unitary and it loses information.

steps: Start with any [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) $U$ on a Hilbert space.
Add the condition that the space is $(\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n}$, the space of $n$ qubits.
Then $U$ is a quantum gate.
links.why: It shows that a quantum gate is a unitary operator on a space of qubits.

reminder: A [field](c:field) $K$ is quasi-algebraically closed when every [homogeneous polynomial](c:homogeneous-polynomial) of degree $d<n$ in $n$ variables has a nontrivial zero in $K^n$.
definition: A [field](c:field) $K$ is quasi-algebraically closed, or $C_1$, when every [homogeneous polynomial](c:homogeneous-polynomial) $f\in K[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ of degree $d$ with $1\le d<n$ has a nontrivial zero in $K^n$. A zero is nontrivial when at least one coordinate is nonzero.
examples: Every finite field is quasi-algebraically closed, by the Chevalley-Warning theorem.
Every [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) is quasi-algebraically closed.
The function field $\mathbb{C}(t)$ is quasi-algebraically closed, which is Tsen's theorem.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}$ is not, because $x^2+y^2+z^2$ has degree $2<3$ but only the trivial zero over $\mathbb{R}$.

steps: Let $K$ be an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) and $f$ a homogeneous polynomial of degree $d$ with $1\le d<n$.
Set $x_3=\dots=x_n=0$, which leaves a binary form $g(x_1,x_2)$.
If $g=0$, the point $(1,0,\dots,0)$ is a nontrivial zero of $f$; otherwise factor $g$ into linear forms over $K$ and solve one of them.
Any such solution is a nontrivial zero of $f$, so $K$ is quasi-algebraically closed.
links.why: It shows that being quasi-algebraically closed is a weaker, degree-bounded form of algebraic closure.

reminder: A quasifibration is a map whose [fibres](c:fiber) are weakly equivalent to its homotopy fibres, with no lifting property required.
definition: A map $p:E\to B$ is a quasifibration when, for every $b\in B$, the inclusion of the [fibre](c:fiber) $p^{-1}(b)$ into the homotopy fibre of $p$ over $b$ is a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence). The homotopy fibre is the [homotopy pullback](c:homotopy-pullback) of $p$ along $\{b\}\to B$. No lifting property is required, in contrast to a [fibration](c:fibration).
examples: Every Serre fibration is a quasifibration.

The projection $(x,y)\mapsto x$ from the L-shape $E=([0,1]\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times[0,1])$ to $[0,1]$ is a quasifibration, because $E$, $[0,1]$ and every fibre are contractible; it is not a fibration, because the path $t\mapsto t$ has no lift that starts at $(0,1)$.
Non-example: the inclusion $S^1\to D^2$ is not a quasifibration, because over the centre of the disc the fibre is empty but the homotopy fibre is equivalent to $S^1$.

steps: Take a [fibration](c:fibration) $p:E\to B$, where a Serre fibration is enough.
For each $b$, the inclusion of the fibre into the homotopy fibre is a weak homotopy equivalence.
This is the defining condition of a quasifibration.
The quasifibration drops the lifting property and keeps only this condition on the fibres.
links.why: It shows that a quasifibration keeps the fibre behaviour of a fibration and gives up the lifting property.

reminder: A Quillen equivalence is a [Quillen adjunction](c:quillen-adjunction) that induces an equivalence of the homotopy categories.
definition: Let $F:\mathcal{M}\rightleftarrows\mathcal{N}:G$ be a [Quillen adjunction](c:quillen-adjunction) between [model categories](c:model-category). It is a Quillen equivalence when, for each cofibrant $A$ in $\mathcal{M}$ and fibrant $X$ in $\mathcal{N}$, a map $FA\to X$ is a [weak equivalence](c:weak-equivalence) exactly when its adjunct $A\to GX$ is one. Equivalently, the derived adjunction is an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories) between the [homotopy categories](c:homotopy-category).
examples: Geometric realization and the singular complex form a Quillen equivalence between simplicial sets and topological spaces.
The Dold-Kan correspondence is a Quillen equivalence between simplicial abelian groups and non-negatively graded chain complexes.

Non-example: the free abelian group functor from simplicial sets to simplicial abelian groups is a Quillen adjunction, but not an equivalence, because it keeps only homology and forgets nonabelian homotopy information.

steps: Start with a [Quillen adjunction](c:quillen-adjunction) $F\dashv G$ between model categories.
It descends to a derived adjunction $\mathbf{L}F\dashv\mathbf{R}G$ between the homotopy categories.
Add the condition that this derived adjunction is an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories).
Then $F\dashv G$ is a Quillen equivalence.
links.why: It shows that a Quillen equivalence is a Quillen adjunction whose derived adjunction is an equivalence.

reminder: A representation of a quiver assigns a vector space to each vertex and a linear map to each arrow.
definition: Let $Q$ be a quiver, that is, a [directed graph](c:directed-graph) with [vertices](c:vertex) $Q_0$ and arrows $Q_1$, its [edges](c:edge), and let $k$ be a field. A representation of $Q$ over $k$ is a family of [vector spaces](c:vector-space) $V_i$ for $i\in Q_0$, together with a [linear map](c:linear-map) $V_a:V_{s(a)}\to V_{t(a)}$ for each arrow $a$ from $s(a)$ to $t(a)$.
examples: For the quiver $1\to2$, a representation is a linear map $V_1\to V_2$.
For the quiver with one vertex and one loop, a representation is a vector space with one endomorphism.
For the Kronecker quiver with two arrows from $1$ to $2$, a representation is a pair of linear maps $V_1\to V_2$.
Non-example: for an arrow from $1$ to $2$, a linear map $V_2\to V_1$ is not allowed, because it goes against the arrow.

steps: Take the quiver with two vertices $1$, $2$ and one arrow $1\to2$.
A representation assigns vector spaces $V_1$, $V_2$ and a [linear map](c:linear-map) $V_1\to V_2$.
So each linear map between vector spaces is a representation of this quiver.
links.why: It shows that quiver representations extend single linear maps to whole networks of maps.

reminder: The quotient ring $R/I$ has the cosets of an [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ as elements, with sum and product computed on representatives.
definition: Let $I$ be a two-sided [ideal](c:ideal) of a [ring](c:ring) $R$. The quotient ring $R/I$ is the set of [cosets](c:coset) $r+I$ with $(r+I)+(s+I)=(r+s)+I$ and $(r+I)(s+I)=rs+I$. These operations are well defined because $I$ is an ideal, and $r\mapsto r+I$ is a surjective [ring homomorphism](c:ring-homomorphism) with kernel $I$.
examples: $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is the quotient of $\mathbb{Z}$ by the ideal $(n)$.
$\mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2+1)\cong\mathbb{C}$, where the class of $x$ plays the role of $i$.

Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ is a subring but not an ideal of $\mathbb{Q}$, and cosets of $\mathbb{Z}$ do not multiply well: $\tfrac12\cdot0=0$ but $\tfrac12\cdot1=\tfrac12$, although $0+\mathbb{Z}=1+\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: Regard $(R,+)$ as an abelian group and the ideal $I$ as a subgroup.
The [quotient group](c:quotient-group) has the cosets $r+I$ as elements and the sum $(r+s)+I$.
Add the condition that $I$ is an ideal, so that $(r+I)(s+I)=rs+I$ is well defined.
Then $R/I$ is a ring whose additive group is that quotient group.
links.why: It shows that a quotient ring is a quotient of the additive group with a product that the ideal makes well defined.

reminder: A quotient space carries the finest topology that makes the projection onto the set of equivalence classes continuous.
definition: Let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space) and $\sim$ an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation) on $X$. The quotient space $X/{\sim}$ is the set of [equivalence classes](c:equivalence-class) with the projection $\pi:X\to X/{\sim}$. A set $U\subseteq X/{\sim}$ is open exactly when $\pi^{-1}(U)$ is open in $X$, which is the finest topology that makes $\pi$ a [continuous function](c:continuous-function).
examples: The circle is $[0,1]/(0\sim1)$, and $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ is also a circle.
The real projective space $\mathbb{RP}^n$ is the quotient of the sphere $S^n$ by $x\sim-x$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ with the topology of $[0,1)$ is not the quotient topology, because $[0,\tfrac12)$ is open there but its preimage in $\mathbb{R}$ is not open.

steps: Take a real or complex vector space $V$ with its usual topology.
Remove the origin and put $v\sim\lambda v$ for nonzero scalars $\lambda$.
Give the set of classes the quotient topology.
The result is the [projective space](c:projective-space) $P(V)$.
links.why: It shows that projective space is one quotient space, a space of lines.

steps: Take a space $X$ and the product $X\times[0,1]$.
Identify all points of $X\times\{0\}$ to one point, and all points of $X\times\{1\}$ to another point.
The quotient topology on the result gives the unreduced [suspension](c:suspension) of $X$.
links.why: It shows that a suspension is a quotient space that collapses the two ends of a cylinder.

reminder: An [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ is radical when $r^n\in I$ for some $n\ge1$ forces $r\in I$.
definition: An [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ is radical when $r^n\in I$ with $n\ge1$ implies $r\in I$, for every $r\in R$. Equivalently, the [quotient ring](c:quotient-ring) $R/I$ has no nonzero nilpotent elements, so its [nilradical](c:nilradical) is zero.
examples: Every [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) is radical, and so is the ideal $(6)$ of $\mathbb{Z}$, which equals $(2)\cap(3)$.
The [vanishing ideal](c:vanishing-ideal) of a set of points in $k^n$ is radical.
Non-example: the ideal $(4)$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ is not radical, because $2^2\in(4)$ but $2\notin(4)$.

steps: Let $P$ be a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) and suppose $r^n\in P$ with $n\ge1$.
If $n=1$, then $r\in P$ at once.
If $n>1$, then $r\cdot r^{n-1}\in P$, so $r\in P$ or $r^{n-1}\in P$ by the prime property.
By induction on $n$ we get $r\in P$ in each case, so $P$ is radical.
links.why: It shows that every prime ideal is radical, so prime ideals are the basic building blocks of radical ideals.

steps: Let $V$ be a set of points in $k^n$ and let $I(V)$ be its [vanishing ideal](c:vanishing-ideal).
Suppose $f^m\in I(V)$ for some $m\ge1$.
Then $f(v)^m=0$ for each $v\in V$, so $f(v)=0$ because $k$ is a field.
So $f\in I(V)$, and $I(V)$ is a radical ideal.
links.why: It shows that the ideals of geometric sets are radical, which is why radical ideals match varieties.

reminder: A random walk adds independent random steps with the same distribution to a starting position.
definition: A random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) with $S_0=0$ and $S_n=S_{n-1}+X_n$, where the steps $X_1,X_2,\dots$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) [random variables](c:random-variable) with the same distribution. It is simple when each step is one of the $2d$ unit vectors $\pm e_i$, each with [probability](c:probability) $1/(2d)$.
examples: The simple random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ has steps $\pm1$ with probability $1/2$ each, like a fair coin game.
The simple random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ moves to one of the four neighbours with probability $1/4$.
Non-example: a walker that flips one coin and then repeats that step forever has equal steps, which are not independent, so it is not a random walk.

steps: Take a random walk $S_n=S_{n-1}+X_n$ with independent steps.
Given the past $S_0,\dots,S_{n-1}$, the next position is $S_{n-1}$ plus a fresh step $X_n$.
Since $X_n$ is independent of the past, the law of $S_n$ depends only on $S_{n-1}$.
So the walk is a [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) whose transition law is the same at every position.
links.why: It shows that a random walk is a Markov chain whose steps do not depend on the position.

reminder: The Rankin-Selberg method integrates a product of two [automorphic forms](c:automorphic-form) against an [Eisenstein series](c:eisenstein-series) to obtain an $L$-function.
definition: Let $f$ and $g$ be [automorphic forms](c:automorphic-form) for a group $\Gamma$ acting on the [upper half plane](c:upper-half-plane) $\mathbb{H}$. The Rankin-Selberg method integrates $f\bar g$ against an [Eisenstein series](c:eisenstein-series) $E(z,s)$ over $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$. Unfolding the Eisenstein series turns the integral into a [Dirichlet series](c:dirichlet-series) in the Fourier coefficients of $f$ and $g$, which is an [L-function](c:l-function) that inherits its analytic continuation from $E(z,s)$.
examples: For two cusp forms of weight $k$ on $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ with Fourier coefficients $a(n)$ and $b(n)$, the method gives $\sum_n a(n)\overline{b(n)}\,n^{-(s+k-1)}$ times a gamma factor.
For $f=g$, the method gives a Dirichlet series with the nonnegative coefficients $|a(n)|^2$.
Non-example: Hecke's method takes the Mellin transform of one form $f$ and also gives $L(s,f)$, but it uses no Eisenstein series, so it is not the Rankin-Selberg method.

reminder: A rate function is a [lower semicontinuous function](c:lower-semicontinuous-function) $I\ge0$ that sets the exponential decay rate of probabilities.
definition: A rate function on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a [lower semicontinuous function](c:lower-semicontinuous-function) $I:X\to[0,\infty]$, and it is good when every set $\{I\le c\}$ is compact. In a [large deviation principle](c:large-deviation-principle), it gives the decay rate of [probabilities](c:probability): $\varepsilon\log P(X_\varepsilon\in A)\to-\inf_A I$ as $\varepsilon\to0$ for nice sets $A$.
examples: For the sample mean of fair $\pm1$ coin flips, $I(x)=\tfrac{1+x}2\ln(1+x)+\tfrac{1-x}2\ln(1-x)$ on $[-1,1]$, and $I=\infty$ outside.
For $dX=b(X)\,dt+\sqrt\varepsilon\,dW$, the Freidlin-Wentzell rate function is $I(\varphi)=\tfrac12\int_0^T|\varphi'-b(\varphi)|^2\,dt$ on absolutely continuous paths $\varphi$ from the start point.
Non-example: $I(0)=1$ and $I(x)=0$ for $x\neq0$ is not lower semicontinuous at $0$, so it is not a rate function.

steps: Start with a [lower semicontinuous function](c:lower-semicontinuous-function) on a topological space $X$.
Require that it takes values in $[0,\infty]$.
Use it in a large deviation principle as the decay rate of probabilities.
Then it is a rate function, and it is good when its sublevel sets are compact.
links.why: It shows that a rate function is a lower semicontinuous function with the role of a decay rate.

reminder: A rational approximation of a real number $x$ is a fraction $p/q$ whose error $|x-p/q|$ is small compared with its denominator $q$.
definition: A rational approximation of a [real number](c:real-number) $x$ is a [rational number](c:rational-number) $p/q$, with [integers](c:integer) $p$ and $q\ge1$, chosen so that the error $|x-p/q|$ is small in terms of the size of $q$. For example, Dirichlet's theorem gives, for each $N\ge1$, a fraction with $1\le q\le N$ and $|x-p/q|<1/(qN)$. The term also covers approximation of a function by rational functions $p(z)/q(z)$ in the uniform norm.
examples: $22/7$ and $355/113$ approximate $\pi$ with errors about $1.3\cdot10^{-3}$ and $2.7\cdot10^{-7}$.
The [continued fraction](c:continued-fraction) convergents $1,2,3/2,5/3,8/5$ of the golden ratio are good rational approximations of it.
Non-example: $\sqrt2$ is not a rational approximation of $\sqrt2$, because it is not a fraction $p/q$.

reminder: In a [directed graph](c:directed-graph), a vertex $t$ is reachable from $s$ when a directed [path](c:path) leads from $s$ to $t$.
definition: Let $G$ be a [directed graph](c:directed-graph) with [vertices](c:vertex) $V$ and [edges](c:edge) $E$. A vertex $t$ is reachable from a vertex $s$ when there is a directed [path](c:path) $s=v_0\to v_1\to\dots\to v_k=t$ with $k\ge0$ and each $(v_{i-1},v_i)\in E$. The reachability problem asks whether $t$ is reachable from $s$ in a given graph.
examples: In the graph $a\to b\to c$, the vertex $c$ is reachable from $a$ and from $b$.
Every vertex is reachable from itself, by the path with $k=0$ edges.
Non-example: in $a\to b\to c$, the vertex $a$ is not reachable from $c$, because the edges point one way.

steps: Read the edges of $G$ as a binary relation $E$ on the vertices.
Take the [transitive closure](c:transitive-closure) of $E$: $u$ is related to $v$ when a path of length $k\ge1$ joins them.
Add the pairs $(u,u)$, which stand for the path with $k=0$.
The result is the reachability relation of $G$.
links.why: It shows that reachability is the reflexive transitive closure of the edge relation.
